prompt.context: Big Green Fuel Systems, a large provider of fuel additives required for the production of gasoline, has recently developed a substantially improved form of ethanol that adds 20% efficiency (measured as miles driven on a single gallon of ethanol). This version of fuel is costly to produce but the market is large and growing more rapidly as increased amounts of ethanol are being used in fuel blends. The company has engaged your team to help determine the viability of this new product, and, if it is viable, how to go about the process of launching it.
prompt.question: Determine the viability of Big Green's new ethanol product and, if viable, recommend how to launch it.

clarifying_info.q: Is the company working in the US only?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, please concentrate on the US market only.

clarifying_info.q: Does the current infrastructure exist to make and support this product?
clarifying_info.a: It is compatible with other infrastructure in the external value chain, but Big Green does not yet have the capacity to mass produce it.

clarifying_info.q: What criteria does Big Green want us to use to determine the viability of the project?
What is the value chain for this product from Big Green to the consumer?
clarifying_info.a: Ethanol is delivered from manufacturers to fuel blenders, who then sell and deliver in bulk to filling stations, who in turn sell it to consumers.

clarifying_info.q: Does Big Green have a patent on this technology?

framework: Standard valuation: assess initial and recurring investment, incremental profit from the venture, and intangible benefits beyond ethanol sales (spin-offs, positive PR)
Barriers analysis: identify internal capability gaps (no mass production capacity) and external pressures across the value chain
Standalone vs. licensed value: determine the product's value operated by Big Green vs. sold/licensed to another more capable company
Competitive response: assess how existing competitors will react and how that manifests throughout the value chain

questions.prompt: Size the US market for ethanol in gallons. There are two ethanol-gasoline blends used in the US: E-85 (85% ethanol, 10% of the market) and E-15 (15% ethanol, 90% of the market). The number of miles driven in the US last year was 1,800 billion miles.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that average fuel mileage is missing and must ask for it. Interviewer provides 20 mpg. Candidate should also ask about the 20% efficiency figure but will be told to ignore it. After calculating, candidate should comment on the size and fragmentation of the market (highly fragmented).

math.setup: Gallons of ethanol = (total miles / avg mpg) * ethanol % * market share for each blend, summed across blends

questions.prompt: The analysis has determined that there is no savings by using this new fuel blend — the fuel costs exactly as much to develop and deliver as can be gained by selling it. The CEO has staked his reputation on this product and is committed to delivering it. How would you best appeal to each level in the value chain to promote this improved product?
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk the value chain from source to consumer and identify distinct value propositions at each level: blenders (reduced blend volume needed, competitive differentiation, lower distribution costs, regulatory positioning), filling stations (eco-sensitive consumer differentiation, PR, fewer refills, potential for smaller tank / new locations), and consumers (eco-friendliness, less time fueling, offset higher per-fill cost by fewer fill-ups).

recommendation: The CEO has committed to rolling out the new fuel. Proceed with launch, leveraging the 20% efficiency gain as the core value proposition throughout the chain.

Appeal to blenders on reduced delivery volumes and competitive/regulatory positioning; appeal to filling stations on eco-differentiation and lower restocking frequency; appeal to consumers on eco-friendliness and time savings at the pump.
risks: Higher sticker price per gallon may create a price-perception problem with consumers even though total spend is comparable due to fewer fill-ups
Marketing investment required to correct the price-perception issue could erode margins
Risk that the new fuel formula is more corrosive than existing fuels, creating liability or infrastructure compatibility concerns
next_steps: Launch a pilot program in a selected market, including targeted marketing efforts, to test the fuel for efficacy and consumer reception
Apply lessons learned from the pilot to a gradual national roll-out
